concepts.name: Election of the President
concepts.description: The electoral college, the weighting of votes, the single transferable vote and disputes about the election (pp.276-279, 295-299).
concepts.idea: The President is chosen indirectly by an electoral college through a weighted single transferable vote.
concepts.rule: The college consists of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament, of the state legislative assemblies and of the assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry (added by the 70th Amendment); nominated members and members of legislative councils do not vote, and members of a dissolved assembly cease to be qualified. An MLA's vote value is the population of the state (1971 census, per the 84th Amendment) divided by the total number of elected members of its assembly, then counted in multiples of one thousand; an MP's vote value is the total value of MLA votes divided by the elected members of both Houses (700 in the 2022 election, from Table 18.4). Voting is by secret ballot, with preferences marked 1, 2, 3; the quota is the valid votes divided by (seats plus one), plus one, and the lowest candidate's votes are transferred until the quota is reached. The Supreme Court decides all disputes; the election cannot be challenged because the college was incomplete, and acts done before a void declaration stay valid. Indirect election was chosen because the President is a nominal executive and direct election would be costly.
concepts.example: In a 2022 college of 4,809 electors (4,033 MLAs and 776 MPs) each MP's vote was worth 700 and a UP MLA's 208, a Sikkim MLA's 7.

questions.q: Which one of the following does NOT form part of the electoral college that elects the President of India?
questions.a: The members of a state legislative council
o: The members of a state legislative council
The elected members of the Legislative Assembly of Delhi
The elected members of the Legislative Assembly of Puducherry
The elected members of the Rajya Sabha
questions.e: p.276: the college is the elected members of both Houses, of the state assemblies and of the assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry; members of state legislative councils, elected or nominated, do not participate.
w: Delhi's elected members were brought into the college by the 70th Amendment and do vote (p.276, p.299).
Only Puducherry's nominated members are excluded; its elected members vote (p.276).
Elected members of both Houses of Parliament form the main part of the college (p.276).

questions.q: In a presidential election the total number of valid votes polled is 9,000 and one candidate is to be elected. Using the quota formula, the quota of votes that a candidate must secure to be declared elected is
questions.e: p.277: the quota is the total valid votes divided by (number of candidates to be elected plus one), plus one; 9,000 / (1 + 1) = 4,500, and adding one gives 4,501.
w: Forgets to add one to the quotient (p.277).
Divides by three, as if two seats were to be filled; the divisor is the number to be elected plus one, i.e. two (p.277).
Divides by the number to be elected alone and adds one; the divisor is the number to be elected plus one (p.277).

questions.q: A state has a population of 2,40,00,000 (1971 census) and 160 elected members in its legislative assembly. Applying the rule for the presidential election, the value of the vote of each of its elected MLAs is
questions.e: p.276: the vote value is the multiples of one thousand in the quotient of the state's population by the total elected members; 2,40,00,000 / 160 = 1,50,000, which holds 150 thousands.
w: Forgets to divide by one thousand: 2,40,00,000 / 160 = 1,50,000, and the multiples of one thousand in it are 150 (p.276).
Divides by ten thousand instead of one thousand (p.276).
Takes the number of elected members as the vote value; the value comes from population divided by members, in thousands (p.276).

w: Acts done before the declaration are not invalidated (p.278).
No parliamentary approval is involved; the Supreme Court's decision is final (p.278).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the electoral college for the presidential election:

1. The elected members of the state legislative councils take part in the election in the states which have such councils.
2. The elected members of the legislative assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry take part in the election.
3. The provision bringing in the assemblies of the Union Territories was added by the 70th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992.
4. The Legislative Assembly of Delhi has no nominated members.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: p.276: members of the state legislative councils, both elected and nominated, do not participate. Statement 2 is correct: p.276 lists them as part of the electoral college. Statement 3 is correct: p.299 (footnote 1): added by the 70th Amendment Act of 1992 with effect from 1 June 1995. Statement 4 is correct: p.276 says so in terms.
w: '1, 2 and 3 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 4, which is correct: p.276
'2 and 4 only' leaves out statement 3, which is correct: p.276
'1, 3 and 4 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.276

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the value of votes in the presidential election:

1. The value of an MP's vote is obtained by dividing the total value of the MLAs' votes by the total number of elected members of the Lok Sabha.
2. All the elected members of the legislative assembly of one state have votes of the same value.
3. In the 2022 election the value of the vote of each Member of Parliament was 543.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is incorrect: p.277: the divisor is the total number of elected members of both Houses of Parliament. Statement 2 is correct: p.276: the number of votes is fixed from the state's population and the total elected members, so it is the same for each member of that assembly. Statement 3 is incorrect: p.299: Table 18.4 gives 5,43,231 / 776 = 700 for each MP.
w: '1 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.277
'1 and 2 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect: p.277
'2 and 3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect: p.277

questions.q:
With reference to the 2022 presidential election, consider the following statements:

1. The electoral college consisted of 4,809 electors, being 4,033 MLAs and 776 MPs.
2. The total value of the votes of the MLAs was exactly equal to the total value of the votes of the MPs.
3. The value of the vote of each MLA of Sikkim was 8.
4. Uttar Pradesh had the highest value for the vote of an MLA, at 208.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: p.299: total electors = MLAs (4033) + MPs (776) = 4809. Statement 2 is incorrect: p.299: the MLAs' total is 5,43,231 and the MPs' total is 5,43,200, close but not equal. Statement 3 is incorrect: p.298: Table 18.4 gives 7 for Sikkim (8 is the figure for Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram). Statement 4 is correct: p.299: Uttar Pradesh is shown at 208, higher than any other state in the table.
w: '1 and 3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 4, which is correct: p.299
'1, 2 and 4 only' includes statement 2, which is incorrect: p.299
'1 and 2 only' includes statement 2, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 4, which is correct: p.299

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about voting in the presidential election:

1. The voting is by secret ballot.
2. Each elector is given only one ballot paper on which preferences are marked as 1, 2, 3 and so on.
3. When no candidate secures the quota on first preferences, the ballots of the candidate with the fewest first preferences are cancelled without any transfer of his second preferences.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: p.277 states that the voting is by secret ballot. Statement 2 is correct: p.277: each member gets only one ballot paper and marks preferences against the names of candidates. Statement 3 is incorrect: p.277: his second preference votes are transferred to the other candidates and the process continues until a candidate gets the quota.
w: '1 and 3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.277
'1, 2 and 3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect: p.277
'2 and 3 only' includes statement 3, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 1, which is correct: p.277

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about disputes and the validity of a presidential election:

2. Members of a dissolved assembly continue to be entitled to vote until fresh elections to that assembly are held.
3. If the Supreme Court declares an election void, acts done by the person before the declaration remain in force.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

w: '1 and 2 only' includes statement 2, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 3, which is correct: p.278

Consider the following statements about why the Constitution makers chose indirect election of the President:

1. Indirect election is in harmony with the parliamentary system, in which the President is only a nominal executive.
2. Direct election would have been costly and consuming of time and energy because of the vast electorate.
3. Election by the two Houses of Parliament alone was not preferred because a Parliament dominated by one party would have picked a President who could not represent the states.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: p.278: giving no real power to a directly elected President would have been anomalous. Statement 2 is correct: p.278 gives this as the second reason. Statement 3 is correct: p.278 gives this as the reason for rejecting election by Parliament alone.
w: '1 and 3 only' leaves out statement 2, which is correct: p.278

1. The election is held by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the manner of voting and counting:

1. The quota is the total valid votes divided by the number to be elected plus one, with one added to the quotient.
2. In the first phase only the first preference votes are counted.
3. A voter must mark a preference against every candidate in the fray for the ballot to count.
4. A candidate with the most first preference votes is declared elected even if short of the quota.

How many of the statements given above are correct?

Statement 4 is incorrect: p.277: a candidate is declared elected only on securing the quota, otherwise transfers begin.

Consider the following statements about the Constituent Assembly's choice of the electoral method:

1. The present system makes the President a representative of the Union and the states equally.

3. Election by the members of the two Houses alone was rejected mainly because it would have been too costly.

How many of the statements given above are correct?
questions.e: Statement 1 is correct: p.278 states this. Statement 2 is incorrect: p.278: some members called it undemocratic and proposed direct election. Statement 3 is incorrect: p.278: it was rejected because a one-party Parliament would choose its own candidate who could not represent the states; cost was the argument against direct election.

'Only two' is not the count: the correct statement(s) are 1 and the incorrect one(s) are 2 and 3, so the number correct is 1: p.278

concepts.name: Qualifications, oath and conditions of office
concepts.description: Eligibility, nomination rules, the oath, conditions of office, emoluments and immunities (pp.279-281, 295).
concepts.idea: The Constitution fixes who may stand, what the President swears and what privileges he holds.
concepts.rule: A candidate must be a citizen of India, at least 35 years old, qualified to be a Lok Sabha member and holding no office of profit (a sitting President, Vice-President, Governor or minister is not deemed to). Nomination needs 50 proposers and 50 seconders and a deposit of Rs 15,000 forfeited below one-sixth of votes; before 1997 these were ten each and Rs 2,500. The oath is administered by the Chief Justice of India or the seniormost Supreme Court judge available. The President may not be a member of a legislature, gets a rent-free residence, and his emoluments, fixed by Parliament, cannot be diminished; the salary was raised to Rs 5 lakh a month in 2018. He is immune from criminal proceedings and arrest during the term and civil proceedings need two months' notice.
concepts.example: A sitting Governor can stand for President, and a sitting MP who wins is deemed to vacate the seat on entering office.

questions.q: A candidate for the office of President loses the security deposit made in the Reserve Bank of India if he fails to secure what share of the votes polled?
questions.e: p.280: the security deposit of Rs 15,000 is liable to be forfeited if the candidate fails to secure one-sixth of the votes polled.
w: A quarter is a higher bar than the text's one-sixth (p.280).
A tenth is a lower bar than the text's one-sixth (p.280).
A third is well above the text's one-sixth (p.280).

questions.q: Before entering upon office the President makes an oath or affirmation, which is administered by the Chief Justice of India. In the absence of the Chief Justice it is administered by
questions.a: the seniormost judge of the Supreme Court available
o: the seniormost judge of the Supreme Court available
the Speaker of the Lok Sabha
questions.e: p.280: the oath is administered by the Chief Justice of India and, in his or her absence, by the seniormost judge of the Supreme Court available.
w: The chapter assigns the oath to the Chief Justice or the seniormost Supreme Court judge (p.280).
The chapter does not give the Speaker this role; it names the seniormost Supreme Court judge available (p.280).
The chapter does not give the Attorney General this role (p.280).

questions.q: Before 1997 a nomination for the office of President had to be subscribed by ten proposers and ten seconders and the security deposit was
questions.e: p.280: before 1997 the proposers and seconders were ten each and the deposit was Rs 2,500; in 1997 they were increased (to 50 each and Rs 15,000).
w: This is the present deposit, raised in 1997 (p.280).
That is double the earlier deposit of Rs 2,500 (p.280).
That is less than the earlier deposit of Rs 2,500 (p.280).

questions.q: A sitting Governor of a state files his nomination for the election of the President. His candidature
questions.a: is not barred, as a Governor is not deemed to hold an office of profit for this purpose
o: is not barred, as a Governor is not deemed to hold an office of profit for this purpose
is barred, as a Governor holds an office of profit under the Union government
is valid only if he is also a sitting Member of Parliament
needs the prior consent of the Election Commission
questions.e: p.280: the holder of an office of profit is not qualified, but a sitting President, Vice-President, Governor or Union or state minister is not deemed to hold one and so can be a candidate.
w: The chapter specifically says a Governor is not deemed to hold an office of profit (p.280).
No such condition exists; the qualifications are those listed on p.280.
The chapter prescribes no such consent (p.280).

questions.q: Which one of the following is NOT a condition of the President's office as laid down by the Constitution?
questions.a: His emoluments may be reduced by Parliament during his term
o: His emoluments may be reduced by Parliament during his term
He should not hold any other office of profit
He may use his official residence without paying rent
He should not be a member of either House of Parliament or of a state legislature
questions.e: p.281: the emoluments and allowances of the President cannot be diminished during the term of office; the other three are conditions listed on p.280.
w: He should not hold any other office of profit (p.280) is a listed condition, so it is not the exception.
The rent-free official residence (p.280) is a listed condition, so it is not the exception.
Not being a member of Parliament or a state legislature (p.280) is a listed condition, so it is not the exception.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the qualifications for election as President:

1. A person must have completed 40 years of age.
2. A person must be qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha.
3. A person must be a citizen of India by birth.
4. A person must not hold an office of profit under the Union, a state, a local authority or any other public authority.

w: '1 and 2 only' includes statement 1, which is incorrect and leaves out statement 4, which is correct: p.280

concepts.name: Term, impeachment and vacancy
concepts.description: Term, re-election, impeachment procedure, vacancies and who acts as President (pp.281-282, 295, 300).
concepts.idea: The President serves five years, can be removed only by a two-House impeachment, and a fixed order of persons fills a vacancy.
concepts.rule: The term is five years from entering office, the President may resign by letter to the Vice-President, continues until the successor assumes charge and is eligible for re-election any number of times. Impeachment is for violation of the Constitution (undefined): charges signed by one-fourth of the members of the originating House, 14 days' notice, two-thirds of the total membership in each House, and the second House investigates with the President entitled to appear. Nominated MPs take part in impeachment, state assembly members do not. concepts.idea: The President's formal powers fall under seven heads, including three kinds of emergency.
concepts.rule: All executive action is taken in his name; he appoints the Prime Minister, ministers, Attorney General, CAG, Election Commissioners and Governors. He summons, prorogues and addresses Parliament, dissolves the Lok Sabha, nominates 12 Rajya Sabha members and needs to recommend Money Bills and certain other bills. He lays the budget, makes advances from the Contingency Fund and constitutes the Finance Commission every five years. He appoints judges, may seek the Supreme Court's non-binding advice and is supreme commander. Emergency powers cover National Emergency (Article 352), President's Rule (Articles 356 and 365) and Financial Emergency (Article 360).
concepts.example: In a national emergency he may suspend Fundamental Rights except those in Articles 20 and 21.

concepts.name: Veto power of the President
concepts.description: The three vetoes over Central and state bills (pp.287-290, 300).
concepts.idea: The President can withhold assent, return a bill or sit on it indefinitely.
concepts.rule: Under Article 111 he may assent, withhold assent or return a non-Money Bill. India has the absolute, suspensive and pocket vetoes but not the qualified veto. The suspensive veto is overcome by re-passage by an ordinary majority; the pocket veto exists because no time limit is prescribed (the USA allows 10 days). He cannot return a Money Bill and has no veto over a constitutional amendment bill. For a bill reserved by a Governor under Article 201 he is not bound to assent even after re-passage.
concepts.example: In 1986 President Zail Singh used the pocket veto on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill.

w: The Indian President has the absolute veto (p.288).

concepts.name: Ordinance-making power
concepts.description: Article 123, its four limitations, judicial review and the Wadhwa case (pp.290-292, 300).
concepts.idea: The President can legislate by ordinance while Parliament is in recess, subject to strict limits.
concepts.rule: An ordinance can be issued when either or both Houses are not in session, has the force of an Act and must be laid before Parliament; it lapses six weeks after reassembly (maximum six months and six weeks). It is coextensive with Parliament's powers, so it cannot take away fundamental rights or amend the Constitution. The President's satisfaction can be questioned for malafide (Cooper, 1970); the 38th Amendment barred this and the 44th deleted the bar. He acts only on ministerial advice; in D.C. Wadhwa (1986) repromulgation was held a violation.
concepts.example: An ordinance can be retrospective and can alter a tax law, but it cannot amend the Constitution.

concepts.name: Pardoning power of the President
concepts.description: Article 72, the five forms of clemency, the Governor's power and the Kehar Singh and Maru Ram principles (pp.285-286, 292-293).
concepts.idea: The President may pardon in court martial, Union-law and death-sentence cases, acting on cabinet advice.
concepts.rule: The power covers sentences by court martial, for offences against Union law and of death, is independent of the judiciary, and the President does not sit as a court of appeal. Pardon removes sentence and conviction; commutation substitutes a lighter form; remission reduces the period; respite gives a lesser sentence for a special fact; reprieve is a temporary stay. The Governor cannot pardon court martial or death sentences but may suspend, remit or commute a death sentence. Kehar Singh (1988): no oral hearing right, evidence may be re-examined, cabinet advice, review only for irrelevance, irrationality, mala fides or discrimination.
concepts.example: A death sentence under a state law can be pardoned only by the President.

w: Remission reduces the period of a sentence without changing its character (p.293).

Reprieve is a temporary stay of execution (p.293).

The Governor can remit a death sentence (p.293).

o: to give relief from an unduly harsh sentence

w: The President does not sit as a court of appeal (p.292).

concepts.name: Constitutional position and discretion of the President
concepts.description: The President as nominal executive, Articles 53, 74 and 75, the 42nd and 44th Amendments and situational discretion (pp.276, 293-296).
concepts.idea: The President is a nominal head who must act on ministerial advice, with narrow situational discretion.
concepts.rule: The real executive is the council of ministers headed by the Prime Minister, collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75); Article 53 vests the executive power and Article 74 binds the President to the advice. The 42nd Amendment (1976) made him bound; the 44th (1978) lets him return the advice once, the reconsidered advice being binding. Ambedkar likened him to the English King, head of State not of the Executive. He has no constitutional discretion but acts on his own in appointing a Prime Minister with no clear majority, dismissing a council without Lok Sabha confidence and dissolving a House when the council has lost its majority.
concepts.example: In 1998 President Narayanan returned a Bihar recommendation, and President's Rule came only after the cabinet repeated it in 1999.

questions.q: The provision that a council of ministers with the Prime Minister at the head shall aid and advise the President, who shall act in accordance with such advice, is contained in
questions.e: p.294: Article 74 provides the council of ministers to aid and advise the President, who 'shall' act in accordance with such advice.
w: Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President (p.294).

Article 78 deals with the Prime Minister's duty to furnish information to the President (p.296).

questions.q: The amendment which authorised the President to require the council of ministers to reconsider its advice, the reconsidered advice being binding on him, is the
questions.e: p.294: the 42nd Amendment (1976) made the President bound by the advice; the 44th Amendment (1978) authorised him to require reconsideration, after which he shall act in accordance with the advice.
w: The 42nd Amendment made the President bound by the advice; it did not add reconsideration (p.294).
The 38th Amendment concerned the finality of the President's satisfaction on ordinances (p.291).
The 24th Amendment made assent to a constitutional amendment bill obligatory (p.289).
